baseline_runs.answer:
- Inflation means prices go up over time, so the same money buys fewer things.
- It happens when lots of people want to buy things, or when making things costs more, like fuel or wages.
- Stores raise prices to keep up, so your dollar doesn't stretch as far as it used to.

runs.answer:

- So the same amount of money buys fewer toys, snacks, or groceries than before.
- It usually happens slowly, and it makes each dollar worth a little less.

- Inflation means prices go up over time.

- Shipping costs more too: trucks, boats, and planes use gas, and getting goods to the store takes more money.
- Prices can rise over time when lots of people want things, and businesses charge more to keep up.

- Making things costs more. Farmers, factories, and workers need more money for fuel, wages, and supplies.
- Money gets weaker. When there's more money around, each dollar buys a little less, so prices go up.
- Companies want to earn money too. Stores raise prices when their costs go up or when people are willing to pay more.

runs.answer:
- Inflation means prices go up over time, so the same amount of money buys a little less stuff than it used to.
- Things cost more when lots of people want to buy them, but there aren't enough to go around, kind of like a popular toy that sells out fast.
- Making things costs more too, like when farmers pay more for fuel or workers need higher pay, and stores pass those costs on to shoppers.

- Inflation means that over time, the same stuff costs more money. A candy bar that cost 50 cents years ago might cost a dollar now.

- Prices go up when lots of people want to buy things, but there isn't quite enough to go around. Stores charge more because they know people will still pay.

- Things can also cost more when it gets more expensive for stores to make and bring their products, like when gas, food, or workers' pay go up. Stores often pass those costs on to you.

runs.answer:
- Inflation means money buys less over time: when prices rise across the board, each dollar gets you fewer things.
- It often happens when more people want to buy things than businesses can make, or when there's more money floating around, so sellers raise prices.
- Costs also push prices up, like when fuel, food, or materials get more expensive for stores to buy.

- Inflation means money buys less over time: when prices rise across the board, each dollar gets you a smaller share of stuff.
- It often happens when lots of people want to buy things at once, or when making and shipping things costs more, so stores raise prices.
- Banks and governments also watch it closely, because if prices rise too fast, everyone's savings and paychecks lose value.
